relations.reason: The reported trial-court findings of government acquisition, preservation, ownership and possession provide lower-court support consistent with the later affirmative Supreme Court title finding. They remain findings from a distinct procedural stage and do not independently execute the Supreme Court's evidentiary assessment.

The protected-monuments register's reported government ownership entry was an express component of the Supreme Court's combined title evaluation, subject to its narrow evidentiary treatment and the absence of independent exhibit authentication.

The Supreme Court's characterization that the manner of acquisition was unchallenged supports its treatment of the register entry as acquisition-related evidence. It does not independently verify the historical acquisition or resolve the broader opposition to government ownership.

The reported CTS entries identifying the government respondent provide additional documentary support for the court's affirmative title evaluation, without independently or conclusively establishing title.

The reported testimony concerning government possession, protected-monument status and construction expenditure formed part of the Supreme Court's conjoint evidentiary assessment. Testimony about possession is not automatically proof of ownership.

The Wakf parties advanced a competing historical and documentary ownership theory inconsistent with exclusive government title. This relation records substantive litigation opposition only; it does not elevate unproved assertions into established counter-title.

The Supreme Court's finding of insufficient concrete evidence undermines the evidentiary substantiation of the Wakf parties' ownership claim. It does not prove their alleged historical events factually false.

The High Court's additional acceptance of adverse possession stands in legal opposition to the Supreme Court's subsequent rejection of that basis. These are distinct judicial-stage determinations, not an unresolved identity or evidence conflict.

The absence of specifically pleaded and proved exclusive possession and animus against the appellant is an expressly identified material deficiency supporting rejection of adverse possession, subject to contextual legal assessment.

The missing specific pleading and proof of the appellant's earlier title undermines the asserted acquisition of another owner's title through adverse possession. The relation does not assert that an earlier title factually never existed.
The missing temporal foundation prevents the record from establishing the relevant commencement and duration of adverse possession. No dispossession date or statutory-period calculation is inferred.

The Supreme Court's requirement of specifically pleaded and proved hostile possession supplies the legal significance of the recorded deficiencies. It does not turn the complete fact-sensitive adverse-possession inquiry into a checklist conjunction.

The original-title assertion and alternative adverse-possession assertion concern the same government claimant and the collectively described disputed properties, raising the renunciation issue. Their simultaneous assertion does not independently establish whether a legally effective renunciation occurred.

The reported precedent makes renunciation of the original-title basis legally relevant to the alternative adverse-possession theory. The legal standard alone does not determine whether renunciation was present, absent or effective in the particular proceedings.

The record does not separately establish whether and when renunciation occurred. This unresolved question cannot be treated as an additional proven reason for rejecting adverse possession; the Supreme Court's identified pleading and proof deficiencies remain independently recorded.

coverage_limits: The fixed reconstruction issue is the distinction between the government claimant's affirmative statutory acquisition-based title and its alternative adverse-possession basis, together with the limited consequence of the courts' identified findings and pleading requirements. The reconstruction stage is SUPREME_COURT_MERITS_APPEAL.

The judgment concerns three related suits and appeals involving CTS No. 24, Karimuddin's Mosque; CTS No. 36, Macca Masjid; and CTS No. 35, Water Tower, all in Bijapur. E4 is a collective reference for the judgment's generalized discussion, not a merger of these properties into a single legal parcel. The source does not always provide an unambiguous parcel-by-parcel mapping of the evidence, findings or party identities.

The affirmative-title evidentiary path corresponds to R1 and R2. F6 records the government ownership entry reported from Exhibit P1, F7 records the Supreme Court's characterization of the acquisition manner as unchallenged, F8 records the relevant CTS entries, F9 records Syed Abdul Nabi's testimony, and F10 records the insufficiency of opposing title evidence. R1 supplies only a narrow acquisition-supporting inference. R2 requires a substantive combined evidentiary evaluation, and its TITLE_ESTABLISHED_ON_RECORDED_EVIDENCE conclusion is not mechanically established by the listed premises. F11 separately records the evaluation actually made by the Supreme Court.

The trial court's reported finding of acquisition as far back as approximately 1900 is preserved separately from the government's asserted title basis under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904. The acquisition date, transaction, statutory mechanism and compliance history cannot be independently reconciled from the supplied record. The judgment also distinguishes acquisition from assumption of guardianship under section 4 as possible explanations for possession; the two mechanisms are not treated as identical.

The principal Wakf opposition is preserved as a party claim: historical religious ownership associated with Peer Mahabari Khandayat, management by successors, alleged sanads, Wakf registration, official notifications and revenue enquiry. F10 records the Supreme Court's finding that concrete supporting title evidence was lacking. This non-proof does not establish that every alleged historical event was false, nor does an unproved counterclaim automatically establish affirmative government title.

The reported trial court findings, High Court findings and Supreme Court findings retain their actual procedural stages. The trial court found government acquisition, preservation, possession, ownership and management; the High Court affirmed the findings and additionally accepted adverse possession; the Supreme Court supported affirmative title but rejected the alternative adverse-possession basis. The different judicial determinations are not collapsed into a single finding.

The adverse-possession path corresponds to R3, R4 and R5. F12, F13 and F14 record three distinct Supreme Court findings of deficient specific pleading and proof: exclusive hostile possession with animus, the appellant's earlier title, and the relevant point of disposition or dispossession. R3's conjunction classifies these particular recorded deficiencies only. It does not implement the complete legal test for acquiring title by adverse possession.

The judgment requires contextual assessment of hostile possession against the true owner, peaceful and open possession, continuity, publicity, extent, actual and visible exclusivity, animus possidendi, the other party's knowledge, commencement, duration and the applicable statutory period. The person claiming adverse possession must clearly plead and establish the necessary facts. R5 remains an OPEN_TEXT semantic evaluation, not a deterministic checklist. The original pleadings, full evidence, relevant historical dates and an independently determined limitation calculation were not supplied.

The judgment recounts precedent that original-title and adverse-possession pleas are mutually inconsistent and that adverse possession does not begin to operate until original title is renounced. F17 preserves the absence of a separately verifiable finding about an effective renunciation and its timing as UNKNOWN, not FALSE. R4 identifies the resulting legal tension without categorically invalidating every alternative adverse-possession pleading. The precedents' independent texts were not examined, and the quoted 12-year discussion is not generalized into a universal statutory rule.

R6 expresses the limited independence of the two bases: the failure of adverse possession does not itself negate an independently established affirmative title ground, and defects in adverse-possession pleading do not themselves prove affirmative title. The Supreme Court's original-title finding is recorded in F11, while its rejection of adverse possession is recorded separately in F18. Neither is established by using the other as a circular premise.

The judgment's accounts of Exhibit P1, Exhibit P2, Syed Abdul Nabi's testimony, opposing historical documents, statutory provisions and cited precedents constitute the supplied evidentiary and legal source. The original exhibits, complete depositions, underlying pleadings, statutory texts and independent precedent judgments were not supplied. No independent authenticity, admissibility, credibility, statutory construction or evidentiary-weight determination has been performed.

The selected six-rule chain has not been independently executed. In particular, R2's OPEN_TEXT title evaluation and R5's OPEN_TEXT adverse-possession evaluation remain unimplemented semantic assessments; R1's documentary inference, R3's recorded-gap classification, R4's renunciation inquiry and R6's limited independence principle do not replace those assessments. The rules are research translations or target-judgment formulations pending qualified legal review, not approved legal rules or human gold findings.

The Supreme Court also addressed the disputed Wakf notifications, additional evidence under Order XLI Rule 27, compliance with section 56 notice, limitation arguments and other statutory issues. These matters are outside the selected title-versus-adverse-possession chain. Their independent analysis is not supplied by the present reconstruction.

F19 preserves the Supreme Court's dismissal of the appeals on April 16, 2004, solely for reconstruction comparison. No relation uses F19 to support any other premise, and no proposed rule makes the appellate disposition its own antecedent. The identified evidence and pleading requirements support the limited distinction between affirmative title and unsuccessful alternative adverse possession; they do not independently implement every legal ground necessary to determine final appellate relief.
